memo.thesis_en: I own three shares of Accenture, bought three days ago at $251.845, and they are now $222.70, down 11.57%. Three days of price tells me nothing about the business, so I'm not going to trade on it. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 26.9% and a debt-to-equity of 0.32. Owner earnings averaged about $9.26 billion against a market cap of about $134 billion, and the model puts value near $437 per share, a 50% margin of safety. That model uses a 5% discount rate and 8% growth, so I'd haircut it. My real worry is whether a people-based services moat holds up against fast technological change, and I can't settle that from this snapshot. I keep the position, I don't add until I've checked the evidence the snapshot lacks, and I don't sell just because Mr. Market is in a mood.

memo.two_paragraph_business_description:
General Dynamics is a defense and aerospace contractor. It designs and builds nuclear submarines and surface ships, armored combat vehicles and munitions, and it supplies information technology and mission systems to the U.S. government and allied customers. It also makes Gulfstream business jets for corporate and private buyers.

It makes money largely by winning long-term, multi-year government contracts, where it is often the sole or primary qualified supplier, and by selling and servicing business aircraft. The defense side offers visibility and sticky relationships, while the aerospace side adds cyclicality and brand pricing power. Little incremental capital is needed relative to earnings, which is why returns on equity run high.
